sections.h2: Which closing charges does Georgia law put on a seller?
sections.html:
One charge is set by the state itself: the real estate transfer tax. Attorney fees, the payoff of your mortgage and any agent commission come from your contract and your lender, so they differ from deal to deal.

Four items have official rules you can read before the day of closing. They are the transfer tax, the PT-61 form that travels with the deed, the property tax for the year, and withholding when the seller lives outside Georgia. The table further down lines them up side by side.

Request a draft settlement statement a few days ahead and check each line against the contract. Georgia lets buyer and seller agree to shift some of these costs, so the contract wording matters.

sections.h2: What is the formula for the Georgia transfer tax?
sections.html:
The state revenue agency bases the tax on the sale price: $1 covers the first $1,000 or any fraction of it, and each further $100 or fraction adds 10 cents. The authority is O.C.G.A. 48-6-1 through 48-6-10.

Liability falls on whoever signs the deed or benefits from it, and the agency's page names the seller as the liable party. The same page notes that contracts often shift the bill to the buyer. If your contract says nothing, the statute leaves it with you, which makes that clause worth reading before you sign.

The clerks' cooperative authority stresses that this is an excise tax on moving title and is separate from the yearly property tax. Paying it settles nothing about your county tax bill.

sections.h2: How does the PT-61 form fit into a Georgia closing?
sections.html:
The PT-61 declares the transfer for tax purposes, and a single form goes with each applicable deed. The filer completes it in the clerks' authority PT-61 eFiling portal, prints a copy, and takes that copy to the Clerk of Superior Court along with the deed documents.

A deed will not be recorded until the transfer tax is paid. After payment, the clerk or a deputy attaches a certification that the tax was paid. Whoever handles your closing normally prepares the form from settlement figures, so your job is to supply accurate sale and parcel details.

For help with the electronic process, the revenue agency lists customer support at (800) 304-5174, or (404) 327-9760 for local callers. Exemption and taxability questions go to the Clerk of Superior Court for the county where the house stands.

sections.h2: Where does the transfer tax money go after the clerk collects it?
sections.html:
The clerk splits it among three levels of government. The revenue agency's page says each Clerk of Superior Court must report the total transfer taxes distributed among the state, the county and the municipalities during the prior calendar year, on a form called FA-RETT, due March 1 each year.

That report is a clerk's duty and does not change what you owe at closing. What it shows is that the transfer tax is shared with the county and any city, and that the certification attached to your deed records that the tax was paid. Ask your settlement agent to confirm that the PT-61 is filed and the tax paid before the documents leave the table.

sections.h2: Who pays the property tax at a Georgia closing?
sections.html:
The person who held title on January 1 answers for that whole year's bill. The state notes that the rule holds even if the sale happens the next day, and that Georgia provides no refund of tax to partial-year owners.

The contract therefore decides how the year gets divided. Most counties set the due date at December 20, though some pick a different one, and taxpayers have 60 days after billing to pay. As one example of a different schedule, Fulton County made most 2026 bills due October 15, with the City of Atlanta's share due September 30.

Steps to take before closing:

  • Ask the county tax commissioner whether the current bill is paid, partly paid or still coming.
  • Ask your settlement agent how the contract splits the year.
  • Check that no county tax lien sits on the clerk's general execution docket, where such liens are filed.

sections.h2: Does the intangible recording tax land on the seller?
sections.html:
It attaches to a new long-term note secured by real estate, so it follows the buyer's financing. The rate is $1.50 per $500 of the note, or part of $500, up to a maximum of $25,000 on one note.

The lender has 90 days to record the security instrument, and the lender may pass the tax along to the borrower. In most counties the Clerk of Superior Court collects it, and a short list of smaller counties uses the tax commissioner or tax collector instead. The buyer's lender is the party that records the new security instrument.

sections.h2: When does Georgia withhold from a nonresident seller?
sections.html:
O.C.G.A. 48-7-128 makes the buyer withhold 3% of the price when the seller lives out of state, or 3% of the gain when the seller provides a sworn gain affidavit. Payment goes in by the end of the month after closing.

The state's exemptions include a principal residence under federal rules, prices below $20,000, and a transfer to a mortgagee in foreclosure with no added payment. Form IT-AFF3, the exemption certificate, is optional but helps the file. The agency's own FAQ describes the charge as income tax withholding.

sections.h2: Which closing records are worth keeping?
sections.html:
Hold on to the final settlement statement, the recorded deed information and any withholding statement the buyer gives you. A nonresident seller attaches the buyer's withholding return, or the equivalent document, to the Georgia income tax return to claim credit.

If a Form 1099-S arrives, the IRS says the sale is reportable even when the gain is excludable, and the settlement statement is what you check its figures against.

  • Final settlement statement showing price, payoff and every charge.
  • The PT-61 copy and the clerk's certificate that transfer tax was paid, when provided.
  • Property tax bill and payment proof for the year of sale.
  • Any Form G-2RP or similar statement of Georgia tax withheld.

faqs.q: Who bears the transfer tax on a Georgia sale?
faqs.a: The seller, under the state's description, unless the contract moves it to the buyer, which is common. Read that clause before signing, since silence leaves the cost with the seller.

faqs.q: What is the Georgia transfer tax rate?
faqs.a: Georgia charges $1 on the first $1,000 and 10 cents on each additional $100, with fractions counted in full. The statutes run from O.C.G.A. 48-6-1 through 48-6-10, and your settlement statement shows the dollar figure.

faqs.q: Can a seller get back property tax after leaving mid-year?
faqs.a: No. The state says the January 1 owner is responsible for the whole year and that no refund goes to partial-year owners. Any split with the buyer happens through the contract.

faqs.q: Who files the PT-61 in Georgia?
faqs.a: The filer completes it online through the clerks' authority portal, and one form goes with each applicable deed. Ask your settlement agent to confirm who is preparing it and that it reaches the clerk with the deed.

faqs.q: Where do I ask about a transfer tax exemption?
faqs.a: Contact the Clerk of Superior Court in the county where the property lies. The state sends taxability and exemption questions there, and the clerk certifies payment before the deed is recorded.
